explanations.answer: For Jesus to make him clean
explanations.explanation: That's the ask, baker. He falls facedown and says, “Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean.” No speeches, no warm-up, just the one request. I think when you're facedown and begging, you get right to the point.

explanations.answer: For Jesus to let him follow
explanations.explanation: Following Jesus is a fine thing to want, friend, but nothing in the text has this man asking for it. His words are “Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean.” He's covered with leprosy, and cleansing is what he begs for. The verse never mentions him wanting to tag along.

explanations.answer: For Jesus to pray for his family
explanations.explanation: That would be a kind thing to ask, baker, but this man doesn't. He's facedown and begging for himself: “…You can make me clean.” His family never comes up in the verse. I think a man in his spot keeps it short and says what he needs.

Look again at his words, friend. He says, “Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean.” He says “You can” plain as day. The only “if” is about whether Jesus is willing, so the man isn't doubting the power. And Jesus answers that “if” right away: “I am willing.” (Luke 5:13)
Right, baker. The man says “…You can make me clean.” He has no doubt about the power. The one “if” is whether Jesus is willing. Then Jesus tells him, “I am willing.” (Luke 5:13)

Yes, baker. Luke says, “And immediately the leprosy left him.” Jesus touches him, says the word, and it's done. Nobody needs a stopwatch. I've waited on cookies my whole life, and this makes me blush.
Sundown would mean a whole day of waiting around, friend. The text doesn't say that. Jesus says, “Be clean!” and the leprosy leaves him right then. Nobody has to keep an eye on the sky.

A whole week of waiting is not what Luke tells us, baker. He says the leprosy left the man “immediately.” Jesus speaks, and that's the moment it goes. Seven days is how long my dough sits when I forget about it.

Jesus says the opposite, friend. His words to the man are “Do not tell anyone,” (Luke 5:14). Instead, He sends him to show himself to the priest. The spreading of the news comes next, and it doesn't come from Jesus telling him to do it.
That's right, baker. Jesus tells the man, “Do not tell anyone.” Then He points him to the priest and the offering Moses prescribed. No town crier job for this man.

Yes, baker. Jesus says, “…go, show yourself to the priest and present the offering Moses prescribed for your cleansing, as a testimony to them.” Moses is Israel's leader who gave the Law. So the man has a stop to make before he does anything else.

No king in this verse, friend. Jesus tells the man to show himself to the priest. The offering is the one Moses, Israel's leader, prescribed for cleansing. I'd have to imagine a whole palace trip, and the text doesn't give one.

Elders are a fair guess, baker, but they aren't who Jesus names. He says to show himself to the priest. That's who gets the offering Moses, Israel's leader, prescribed for his cleansing. One name in the verse, and it's the priest.

explanations.answer: To hear Him and be healed
explanations.explanation: That's what Luke says, baker: “…great crowds came to hear Him and to be healed of their sicknesses.” Two reasons, and both are right there in the verse. The news about Jesus is traveling, and people are showing up. I'd be checking if I had enough chairs.

explanations.answer: To crown Him as their king
explanations.explanation: Luke doesn't say that, friend. The crowds came “…to hear Him and to be healed of their sicknesses.” A crown never comes up in this verse. They came to listen and to be made well.

explanations.answer: To see the man who was healed
explanations.explanation: That's a reasonable thing to guess, baker, but it isn't what the text says. It says the news about Jesus spread, and the crowds came “…to hear Him and to be healed of their sicknesses.” The reasons are about Jesus Himself. Hearing and healing are the two things named.

Yes, baker. Luke says, “Yet He frequently withdrew to the wilderness to pray.” The crowds are great, and still Jesus goes off to pray. If a crowd like that showed up at my bakery, I'd be doing a victory dance on my gold base.
The text says otherwise, friend. “Yet He frequently withdrew to the wilderness to pray.” Great crowds are coming, and Jesus keeps heading out to pray. That's what the verse tells us.

Right, baker. Luke says, “…the power of the Lord was present for Him to heal the sick.” The room has teachers, visitors from all over, and that power is right there. Something is about to happen in that house.

Luke says the opposite, friend. He writes, “…the power of the Lord was present for Him to heal the sick.” It's right there while Jesus teaches. The room is full of people who came from Jerusalem and from every village of Galilee and Judea.

Yes, baker. Luke says, “…they could not find a way through the crowd.” The place is packed, and there's no gap to squeeze through. I get it. I once tried to reach the last cookie at a full counter and gave up.
No door trouble is mentioned, friend. Luke says, “…they could not find a way through the crowd.” The crowd is what stops them. Nobody mentions a key, which is good news for a key I once knew.

The Pharisees are in the room, baker. Luke says they were sitting there. But what blocks the men is stated plainly: “…they could not find a way through the crowd.” The text doesn't say the Pharisees stopped them.

He doesn't land at the back, friend. Luke says the men lowered him “…into the middle of the crowd, right in front of Jesus.” That's the whole point of the roof. They came in from above, and they landed him right where they wanted.
Yes, baker. They lowered him “…into the middle of the crowd, right in front of Jesus.” Not the back row, not the side. Right in front. Those men were not settling for a seat near the exit.

That's it, baker. Luke says, “When Jesus saw their faith, He said…” The men had been carried through a roof's worth of effort, and Jesus sees it. The word is faith. I'd have to pause my mixer for that one.
Money never comes up in this scene, friend. Luke says, “When Jesus saw their faith, He said…” What Jesus sees is their faith. Nobody mentions a coin or a pocket.
I'd bet they had some worry, baker, but that's only my guess. The text says, “When Jesus saw their faith, He said…” Faith is the word Luke gives us. Worry isn't mentioned at all.

Yes, baker. Jesus says to him, “Friend, your sins are forgiven.” That's the first thing He says to the paralyzed man. I'd have guessed something else for opening words, so I'm glad I'm not writing this script.

It really is the first thing, friend. Luke says Jesus saw their faith and said, “Friend, your sins are forgiven.” Those are His first words to the man. I'd have guessed something else too, so don't feel alone.
Yes, baker. The scribes and Pharisees think, “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” They're only thinking it, and nobody says it out loud. And Jesus knows what they are thinking.
Priests are a fair guess, friend, but that's not their thought. They think, “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” The word they use is God. The text doesn't mention priests in their thinking.
Moses is Israel's leader, baker, and he's a big name. But that's not who the scribes and Pharisees name in their thoughts. They think, “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” God alone is the phrase.

Right, baker. Jesus says, “But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on the earth to forgive sins…” Son of Man is the name Jesus uses for Himself (Mark 2:10). Then He turns to the paralyzed man. That sentence is the whole point.

That isn't what Jesus says, friend. He says the Son of Man “…has authority on the earth to forgive sins…” Son of Man is the name Jesus uses for Himself (Mark 2:10). Priests never come up in His sentence.
Not in this verse, baker. Jesus says the Son of Man “…has authority on the earth to forgive sins…” Son of Man is the name Jesus uses for Himself (Mark 2:10). Nothing here mentions rewriting the Law.

explanations.answer: Pick it up and go home
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says, “…get up, pick up your mat, and go home.” Three things in one sentence, and the mat is the middle one. A man who couldn't move is given a to-do list.
He isn't told to leave it, friend. Jesus says, “…get up, pick up your mat, and go home.” The mat goes with him. Luke even says he “took what he had been lying on.” (Luke 5:25)
His friends carried him in, baker, so that's a fair guess. But Jesus says, “…get up, pick up your mat, and go home.” The man picks it up himself. The text doesn't have him handing it off.
Yes, baker. Luke says the man “…went home glorifying God.” He walks out on his own two feet, and the praise goes with him. I'd be glorifying God too, and probably a little loudly.
His friends did a lot, friend. They went through a roof for him. But the text says he “…went home glorifying God.” That's what Luke tells us he's doing on the way.
His family doesn't show up in this passage, baker. Luke says he “…went home glorifying God.” That's what he does on the way. The text gives him that one thing.

The text says otherwise, friend. Luke writes, “Everyone was taken with amazement and glorified God.” They were “…filled with awe and said, ‘We have seen remarkable things today.’” That doesn't sound unsure to me.
Yes, baker. “Everyone was taken with amazement and glorified God.” They said, “We have seen remarkable things today.” They knew they'd seen something remarkable.
